phase.label: Kristiania Bohème, mid-1880s — his first “soul painting”

source.label: Wikipedia: The Sick Child (1886) was his first “soul painting”, his first break from Impressionism
Wikipedia: The Sick Child (Munch) — built up from thick layers of impasto paint

highlight.text: The painted versions are built up from thick layers of impasto paint with heavy, broad vertical brushstrokes. The emphasis on verticals gives the works a hazy feel and adds to their emotive power

source.label: Wikidata: The Sick Child (NG.M.00839), oil paint on canvas

work.text: In the space of that year [1885 – 1886], scratching it out, just letting the paint flow, endlessly I tried to recapture what I had seen for the first time – the pale transparent skin against the linen sheets, the trembling lips, the shaking hands. I repainted the painting numerous times – scratched it out – let it become blurred in the medium – and tried again and again to catch the first impression

work.text: I started as an Impressionist, but during the violent mental and vital convulsions of the Bohême period Impressionism gave me insufficient expression—I had to find an expression for what stirred my mind … The first break with Impressionism was the Sick Child—I was looking for expression.

source.author: Edvard Munch
source.title: Writings on the origin of the Frieze of Life, quoted in “The Sick Child (Munch)”
source.license: Short excerpt of an English translation, via Wikipedia (CC BY-SA)

moment.text: It came into being during the period of the indurated worship of reality that stamped the eighties. The picture, moreover, was a veritable gauntlet cast in the face of [photographic] realism; it was sheer feeling, enveloped in a veil of lovely color.

moment.text: There is genius in Munch. But there is also the danger that it will go to the dogs … For this reason, for Munch's own sake, I would wish that his Sick Child had been refused … In its present form this 'study'(!) is merely a discarded half-rubbed-out sketch.

matters.text: When Edvard Munch was thirteen years old, his sister Sophie died of tuberculosis. … Munch later described the process of painting these works as a form of technical and personal catharsis.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago

matters.text: few painters have ever experienced the full grief of their subject as I did in 'The sick child'. It was not just I who was suffering; it was all my nearest and dearest as well.

source.author: Edvard Munch
